research_question: Which canid and funerary iconographies can visually confound Sobek classification, and which modern retellings of the Sobek-Horus-Osiris-Ra narratives survive source checking against ancient texts, museum records, and academic reference translations?

source_policy.tier_A: official museum records, UCL Digital Egypt / Petrie Museum records, direct translations or catalogued ancient texts
source_policy.tier_B: ancient classical witnesses such as Plutarch, explicitly marked as late and non-uniform with pharaonic Egyptian sources
source_policy.tier_C: modern encyclopedic, tourism, blog, social-media and fandom retellings; retained only as discovery leads, never sufficient for promotion
source_policy.rule: A modern retelling is not converted into canonical JANUS evidence when a higher-tier source differs, is silent, or shows multiple variants.

anubis_canid_control.reason: Low-resolution, damaged, highly schematic, or algorithmically reduced silhouettes can confuse an elongated canid muzzle with a crocodilian snout even though the canonical animal morphologies are distinct.
anubis_canid_control.important_refinement: The strongest ancient iconographic ambiguity is often within the canid class itself: Anubis, Wepwawet and sometimes other canid-headed deities can share a jackal/canid morphology. Therefore the control must not be named ANUBIS_ONLY; it must include a broader CANID_DEITY_CONTROL class.

museum_grounding.claim: Anubis appears in full animal form as a recumbent canid/jackal-like animal.
Anubis appears as a striding anthropomorphic male with a jackal/canid head.
Ancient artists did not necessarily distinguish modern zoological canid species in divine representations; a canid head could fit Anubis, Duamutef or Wepwawet depending on context.
UCL distinguishes Sobek as crocodile power and Anubis as an embalming deity shown jackal-headed.
A jackal-headed amuletic deity may be Anubis or Wepwawet, demonstrating a real within-canid identification ambiguity.

CANID: paws/long mammalian legs in full animal form
recumbent jackal/canid posture frequent in funerary contexts
CROCODILIAN: long broad or flattened crocodilian rostrum
absence of tall pointed canid ears
low elongated reptilian body when full animal is shown

blind_test_requirement.promotion_rule: Sobek crocodilian-core classification must remain specific after inclusion of canid-deity controls; errors must be reported by confusion pair rather than collapsed into a generic false-positive rate.

myth_claim_ledger.submitted_claim: Ra was divided and asked Sobek to gather his body parts.
myth_claim_ledger.reason: The source-audited narrative found for Ra and Sobek is Book of the Dead 113 / Coffin Text 158, where Ra summons Sobek to recover Horus's hands/arms from the water, not pieces of Ra.

myth_claim_ledger.submitted_claim: Osiris was killed and dismembered by Seth and his body was reassembled by Isis/Nephthys.
myth_claim_ledger.reason: Museum and Egyptian textual traditions strongly support the murder/dismemberment and restoration complex.

myth_claim_ledger.submitted_claim: Seth cut Osiris into exactly 14 pieces.
myth_claim_ledger.reason: Fourteen is prominent in the much later Greek-language Plutarch tradition, while Egyptian sources and later cult topographies vary in body-part enumeration and localization. The dismemberment is robust; the fixed number 14 is not a universal invariant for JANUS analysis.

myth_claim_ledger.submitted_claim: Ra asks Sobek to retrieve the lost hands/arms of Horus from the water; Sobek catches them with a net/snare.
myth_claim_ledger.reason: Book of the Dead 113, descending from Coffin Text 158, explicitly has Ra summon Sobek, Sobek fish/search for the scattered hands/arms, and the snare/net act as an aetiology.

myth_claim_ledger.submitted_claim: Seth cut off both hands of Horus and threw them into the Nile in the narrative used by Book of the Dead 113.
myth_claim_ledger.reason: The UCL translation begins the episode with 'what his mother did to him' and does not identify Seth as the amputator. Modern secondary summaries commonly connect the episode with Isis removing Horus's contaminated hands after the sexual-conflict episode. Therefore Seth-as-amputator must not be frozen into the canonical ledger without a separate primary witness.

myth_claim_ledger.submitted_claim: Sobek invented the first fishing net and taught humans to fish.
myth_claim_ledger.reason: BD113 gives an aetiological statement for the snare/net in the recovery of Horus's hands. The stronger statement that Sobek explicitly taught humanity fishing is not stated in the UCL passage and should remain secondary unless independently sourced.

myth_claim_ledger.submitted_claim: Sobek swallowed one or more parts of Osiris and had his tongue cut out as punishment.
myth_claim_ledger.reason: A damaged Coffin Text 991 line has been interpreted by some scholars/secondary discussions in this direction, but the reading is conjectural. In Plutarch's late version, fish consume the missing phallus; Sobek is not the eater. This item is retained as a disputed tradition marker, not canonical narrative fact.

myth_claim_ledger.submitted_claim: The Eye of Horus is wounded/lost in conflict and restored, becoming a symbol of healing and regeneration.
myth_claim_ledger.reason: Museum and Egyptian text records support damage to the Eye of Horus and its restored/protective meaning. Exact mechanics vary by textual tradition and must not be collapsed into one universal story.

myth_claim_ledger.submitted_claim: Seth tears Horus's left lunar eye into pieces and Thoth reassembles it; this is the single canonical version.
myth_claim_ledger.reason: Ancient sources preserve several injury/restoration variants. For example BD112 describes Seth as a black boar causing eye injury, while other conflict traditions describe different eye injuries. JANUS must model narrative variants separately rather than forcing a single event sequence.

myth_claim_ledger.submitted_claim: The Eye of Horus can be transferred/offered in an Osirian funerary context and participates in restoration/rebirth symbolism.
myth_claim_ledger.reason: The Eye of Horus is repeatedly an offering/restorative object in funerary ritual, and texts place it with/protecting Osiris. This supports a strong Horus-eye-to-Osirian-restoration bridge without requiring one oversimplified narrative sentence.

myth_claim_ledger.submitted_claim: There is a separate standard 'Eye of Osiris' iconographic symbol, distinct from the Eye of Horus, typically represented by ordinary human eyes on coffins and functioning as Osiris's all-seeing judicial eye.
myth_claim_ledger.reason: Middle Kingdom coffin eye panels are explicitly described by museum sources as Horus/wedjat eyes or magical eyes through which the deceased could see the rising sun. They should not be relabelled as a separate standard 'Eye of Osiris' class without object-specific inscriptional evidence. The 'all-seeing judicial eye of Osiris' formulation is therefore retained only as a modern interpretive claim, not ancient iconographic fact.

high_confidence_edges: SETH -> injures -> HORUS_EYE in attested variants
variant_or_uncertain_edges: ISIS -> removes -> HORUS_HANDS in one interpretive lineage
THOTH -> restores -> HORUS_EYE in some traditions
SOBEK -> swallows -> OSIRIS_PARTS is textually uncertain

protocol_amendment_for_sobek_v0_2.critical_test: Crocodilian-core features must outperform crown-only features and remain specific against canid controls under held-out periods and low-resolution stress conditions.
no_promotion_until: exact museum source images are sealed
identity labels are hidden during feature extraction

highest_admissible_claim: The Sobek research line must add a canid-deity confusion class because low-resolution or schematic animal-headed figures can produce Sobek-vs-canid errors even though canonical crocodilian and canid morphologies are distinct. Source checking also separates several modern myth conflations: Book of the Dead 113 has Sobek recover Horus's hands/arms at Ra's request; Osiris, not Ra, is the robust dismembered deity; the fixed fourteen-part count is not a universal pharaonic constant; and Middle Kingdom coffin eyes are normally Horus/wedjat eyes rather than a separate default 'Eye of Osiris' iconographic class. These corrections strengthen, rather than weaken, the future blind modular-iconography test by preventing label leakage and narrative conflation.
